title: Houthis Strike Saudi Tanker in Red Sea as Hormuz Route Deal Takes Shape; Belarus Fuel Exports to Russia Hit Record; US Locks Down Critical Mineral Scrap
subhead: Iran and Oman agree on Hormuz shipping route coordinates — but Tehran warns it alone won't guarantee security. Meanwhile, Houthis hit a Saudi tanker hundreds of kilometers from their declared blockade zone, Belarus replaces Russian refinery output lost to Ukrainian drones, and the US bans tungsten and battery black mass exports to keep critical minerals at home.

sections.heading: Iran-Oman Agree on Hormuz Route Coordinates — But Security Remains Unresolved
sections.body:
Iran and Oman have reached an 'understanding on the geographical coordinates of the route under discussion' for commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei announced on Wednesday, according to The Guardian. Baghaei described the negotiations as 'professional' and 'moving forward,' saying a joint statement was in the 'final stages of review and drafting,' provided that 'some third parties do not obstruct the process.'

But the deal carries a significant caveat: Baghaei explicitly said the agreement alone would not guarantee security in the strait. According to Reuters, a senior Iranian source and two regional officials said the proposed arrangement would give Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf through Hormuz — one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran. President Trump claimed a broader US-Iran peace deal could come 'as soon as Wednesday,' though the Iranian and regional sources pushed back, saying important details still had to be agreed.

The coordinates reportedly merge Iran's proposed northern corridor with the Omani-managed southern route, with Iran retaining control of inbound traffic — the very arrangement Tehran has sought since the war began. Oil prices slipped on Thursday, with Brent hovering near $80 as markets priced in de-escalation hopes, according to Reuters. But tanker traffic through Hormuz remains subdued despite the diplomatic progress, OilPrice reported, suggesting that shipping companies are not yet betting on a quick normalization.
sections.whyItMatters: The route agreement is a genuine diplomatic step, but Iran's caveat that it doesn't guarantee security — combined with control over inbound traffic — means the strait's reopening would come on Tehran's terms. Markets are cautiously optimistic; shippers are not.

sections.heading: Houthis Hit Saudi Tanker Far From Blockade Zone — Red Sea Threat Expands
sections.body:
Yemen's Houthi movement claimed a 'precise hit' with ballistic missiles on the Saudi-flagged products tanker NCC WAFA off Yanbu in the northern Red Sea, hundreds of kilometers from the group's declared blockade zone around Bab el-Mandeb. According to maritime intelligence group Windward, the vessel had gone dark on July 19, likely U-turned after the July 22 blockade announcement, and was heading back north through Saudi coastal waters 'where the missiles found her anyway.'

Windward's analysts noted: 'The Houthi statement explicitly tied the strike to Saudi tankers rerouting north to avoid Bab el-Mandeb, and vowed escalation in the northern Red Sea regardless of consequences.' The Houthis say they have targeted a total of 8 Saudi tankers since the blockade began and intercepted or forced back as many as 29 Saudi oil tankers. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed the strike on the Wafaa.

The attack demonstrates that the Houthi threat extends well beyond Bab el-Mandeb — tankers rerouting north through the Red Sea are now being hit too. Saudi Arabia has rerouted some exports toward Egypt and the Suez Canal, while other vessels transit Bab el-Mandeb in dark mode. Oil prices briefly rebounded above $80 on the news before settling back, according to RTE and multiple market sources.
sections.whyItMatters: The strike on a tanker near Yanbu — roughly 1,000 km north of Bab el-Mandeb — shows the Houthis can reach vessels attempting to evade their declared blockade zone. Rerouting north is no longer a safe mitigation. This compresses Saudi export options to Suez and the East-West pipeline further.

sections.heading: Belarus Fuel Exports to Russia Hit Record as Ukrainian Drones Cripple Refineries
sections.body:
Gasoline and diesel supplies from Belarus to Russia hit a new monthly record in July, according to Reuters, as fuel shortages driven by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries forced Moscow to import from its neighbor. Gasoline shipments by rail rose 13% from June to 212,000 metric tons, while diesel deliveries doubled to 162,000 tons. Over the first seven months of 2026, Belarusian rail gasoline shipments to Russia surged 25-fold compared to the same period in 2025, reaching nearly 665,000 tons, Reuters calculated. Diesel deliveries increased almost sevenfold to 418,000 tons.

Belarus processes Russian crude at its two refineries, which hold a combined capacity of 480,000 barrels per day. Russia has also begun importing gasoline from India, Kazakhstan, and Morocco, according to industry sources cited by United24 Media. Russian gasoline output fell to roughly 65% of the seasonal average in early July, while diesel production dropped to about domestic demand levels. The Russian government has banned diesel exports, extending restrictions already in place on gasoline and jet fuel. In a telling move, Moscow also authorized Euro-2 gasoline through July 1, 2027 — a lower-grade fuel previously banned for environmental reasons — to prevent outright shortages.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's drone campaign has done what months of sanctions could not: force Russia to become a net fuel importer from its own client state and from countries as far as India and Morocco. The 25-fold increase in Belarusian gasoline shipments to Russia is a direct measure of how much refinery capacity has been lost.

sections.heading: US Bans Tungsten and Battery Black Mass Exports to Secure Critical Mineral Supply
sections.body:
The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security published an interim final rule on August 5 restricting exports of tungsten scrap and black mass — shredded metals from recycled lithium-ion batteries — for one year without a license. The rule, effective August 27, implements a Defense Production Act presidential determination from last week declaring recoverable critical minerals 'scarce and essential to the national defense.'

The move comes as tungsten prices have surged over 500% in the past year due to Chinese export restrictions, tight global supply, and heavy military spending, OilPrice reported. The US also recently confirmed its largest known tungsten resource in Nevada, though development faces opposition from NASA, which says mining would interfere with satellite tracking operations in the area. Separately, India is pushing to build a domestic rare-earth magnet industry after China's export curbs exposed a critical vulnerability — but lacks the integrated industrial capacity to convert raw rare earths into finished magnets, the Financial Express reported.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is now treating recycled battery metals and tungsten waste with the same export-control rigor as weapons-grade technology. With tungsten up 500% and China restricting exports, the question isn't just about supply — it's about whether domestic processing capacity can scale fast enough to replace the Chinese refining pipeline that the world has relied on for decades.

sections.heading: China Eases Fuel Export Curbs for Second Month as Global Supply Squeezes
sections.body:
China has eased limits on refined fuel exports for a second consecutive month in August, granting refiners temporary approval to ship 2.7 million metric tons of oil products to destinations excluding Hong Kong and Macau, Reuters reported on August 5 citing industry sources. China had slashed fuel exports from March through June to protect domestic supplies after the Iran war disrupted crude flows and forced a sharp cut in imports. The easing signals Beijing's assessment that domestic supply is now more secure — or that the revenue opportunity from elevated global refining margins is too significant to pass up.

China's move coincides with record global refining margins. Phillips 66 reported Q2 earnings of $3.85 billion, up from $207 million in Q1, with realized refining margins jumping from $10.11 to $24.08 per barrel. The company expects strong margins to continue through 2027, citing sustained supply disruptions from the Iran war. Marathon Petroleum posted $8.5 billion in adjusted EBITDA. The global refining margin surge is a direct consequence of the Middle East conflict removing roughly 20% of world oil supply transit from the market, creating a windfall for refiners with access to non-Gulf crude.
sections.whyItMatters: China's fuel export easing and the record refining margins at US refiners are two sides of the same coin: the Middle East conflict has created a massive geographic arbitrage in refined products. Refiners with access to stable crude flows are printing money while Gulf-dependent supply chains remain disrupted.

sections.heading: Iraq-Syria Pipeline Could Bypass Hormuz Within Three Years
sections.body:
A senior Syrian official says the old Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline from Iraq to Syria's Mediterranean coast could be up and running within three years, OilPrice reported. Youssef Qablawi, CEO of Syria's state-owned Petroleum Company, said engineering studies and material procurement would be followed by construction taking 30 months to three years. The project envisions two pipelines with capacity of 1.5-2 million barrels per day, and the US has voiced support for the plan as a way to diminish Iran's leverage over Hormuz-dependent exports. US companies are expected to participate in the reconstruction.

Iraq desperately needs export routes that bypass Hormuz. The strait's closure forced OPEC's second-largest producer to slash upstream production, costing Baghdad billions in lost revenue. Meanwhile, Venezuela's crude production surpassed 1 million barrels per day in June 2026, according to OilPrice — driven by sanctions relief, regulatory changes, and the Middle East supply disruption that has made every non-Gulf barrel more valuable. India's ONGC is also preparing to resume operations at two Venezuelan oil projects, taking over operatorship as sanctions ease.
sections.whyItMatters: The Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline is a concrete response to the Hormuz crisis: a 1.5-2 million bpd alternative that removes Iraqi dependency on the strait entirely. But three years is a long time in a conflict zone, and Syria's post-war governance raises questions about security of supply. Venezuela crossing 1 million bpd is a reminder that the Middle East disruption is reshaping global supply hierarchies in real time.

sections.heading: Aramco's Record Profits Mask a Widening Cash Flow Gap
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco posted $33.4 billion in adjusted net income for Q2 2026 and $67.2 billion for the first half — figures that make it the world's most profitable energy company. But the real story is in the cash flow: Q2 free cash flow was just $12.3 billion against a base dividend commitment of $21.9 billion, meaning cash covered only about 56% of shareholder distributions. Over the first half, cumulative free cash flow of $30.9 billion fell $13 billion short of dividend commitments, according to analysis by OilPrice contributor Cyril Widdershoven.

Realized crude prices jumped from $76.90/barrel in Q1 to $108.10/barrel in Q2, yet operating cash flow actually declined from $30.7 billion to $25.4 billion. Aramco transferred over $87 billion to the Saudi state in H1 2026 through taxes, royalties, and dividends — effectively functioning as the Kingdom's financial backbone. The company has also highlighted 'unfavorable movements in amounts due from the Saudi government' as a factor affecting cash conversion. Downstream EBIT doubled to $6.2 billion on improved refining margins, and capital expenditure rose to $13.2 billion.
sections.whyItMatters: Aramco's profit surge is a war premium dividend — but the gap between accounting profit and available cash is widening fast. The company is now the financial transmission mechanism linking global oil markets directly to Saudi public finances and Vision 2030. If oil prices retreat, the $13 billion half-year cash shortfall becomes a structural problem.

bottomLine: August 6 brought a day of contradictory signals. Iran and Oman agreed on shipping route coordinates for Hormuz — the most tangible progress yet on reopening the strait — but Tehran warned the deal alone doesn't guarantee security, and the terms would give Iran control over inbound traffic. Meanwhile, the Houthis demonstrated they can hit Saudi tankers 1,000 km north of Bab el-Mandeb, closing off the main rerouting option Saudi Arabia had left. Russia is now importing fuel from Belarus at a 25-fold increase over last year, a direct consequence of Ukraine's drone campaign. The US locked down tungsten and battery scrap exports under the Defense Production Act as tungsten prices surged 500%. And Aramco's record profits conceal a $13 billion half-year cash shortfall that makes the Kingdom's fiscal model look increasingly fragile. The pattern is clear: every diplomatic step forward is matched by a military or financial reality pulling in the opposite direction.
sources: The Guardian, Reuters, OilPrice, Windward, United24 Media, CSIS, Financial Express, RTE, CNBC, Seeking Alpha, Yahoo Finance, Al Bawaba, Hydrocarbonprocessing, 3 Proton Lithium/PR Newswire, India TV News, US Commerce Department/BIS, Presidential Determination on Recoverable Critical Minerals
